questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The nutrient class made up of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, serving as the body's primary and quickest source of energy, is
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates, composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, are the body's main and most readily available source of energy.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The nutrient class primarily responsible for growth, repair, and maintenance of body tissues is
questions.explanation: Proteins provide the amino acids essential for building, repairing, and maintaining body tissues, including muscles and organs.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The nutrient class that provides the most concentrated source of energy per gram, and also supplies essential fatty acids, is
questions.explanation: Fats and lipids provide over twice the energy per gram compared to carbohydrates or proteins, and also supply essential fatty acids.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A deficiency disease caused by insufficient dietary protein, especially common in children, characterised by swelling (oedema) and stunted growth, is called
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor results from severe protein deficiency, often marked by oedema (swelling), a distended belly, and growth impairment, primarily in children.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A deficiency disease caused by insufficient vitamin C, characterised by bleeding gums and poor wound healing, is called
questions.explanation: Scurvy results from prolonged vitamin C deficiency, causing symptoms such as bleeding gums, joint pain, and poor wound healing.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A deficiency disease caused by insufficient vitamin D (or calcium), leading to soft, weak, and deformed bones in children, is called
questions.explanation: Rickets results from vitamin D deficiency, impairing calcium absorption and leading to soft, weak bones in growing children.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A deficiency disease caused by insufficient vitamin B1 (thiamine), affecting the nervous system and heart, is called
questions.explanation: Beriberi results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, affecting the nervous and cardiovascular systems.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Vitamins that dissolve in water and are generally not stored in significant amounts in the body, requiring regular dietary intake, include
options: vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins
questions.explanation: Water-soluble vitamins, such as vitamin C and the B-complex group, are not significantly stored in the body and must be consumed regularly.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Vitamins that dissolve in fat and can be stored in the body's fatty tissues for longer periods include
options: vitamins A, D, E, and K
questions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) can be stored in the body's fat tissues, unlike water-soluble vitamins which require more regular intake.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Minerals required by the body in relatively large amounts, such as calcium and phosphorus, are classified as
questions.explanation: Macro (major) minerals, including calcium, phosphorus, and sodium, are needed by the body in comparatively larger amounts.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Minerals required by the body only in very small amounts, such as iron and zinc, are classified as
questions.explanation: Trace elements (micro minerals), such as iron, zinc, and iodine, are essential but required only in small quantities.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Water is considered an essential nutrient mainly because it
options: regulates body temperature, transports nutrients, and supports many metabolic processes
is only needed by the very young
questions.explanation: Water plays vital roles in temperature regulation, nutrient transport, waste removal, and many essential metabolic processes, despite providing no calories itself.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The breakdown of food through physical actions such as chewing and the churning of the stomach is called
questions.explanation: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces through actions like chewing and stomach churning, increasing surface area for chemical digestion.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The breakdown of food through the action of enzymes and digestive juices into simpler chemical substances is called
questions.explanation: Chemical digestion uses enzymes and other digestive secretions to break complex food molecules down into simpler, absorbable substances.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Enzymes that break down starches (carbohydrates) into simpler sugars are called
questions.explanation: Amylases are digestive enzymes that specifically break down starches into simpler sugar molecules.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Enzymes that break down proteins into smaller peptides and amino acids are called
questions.explanation: Proteases are digestive enzymes that break down proteins into smaller peptide chains and individual amino acids.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Enzymes that break down fats into fatty acids and glycerol are called
questions.explanation: Lipases are digestive enzymes specifically responsible for breaking down fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The process by which digested nutrients pass through the wall of the small intestine into the bloodstream is called
questions.explanation: Absorption is the process by which broken-down nutrients move across the intestinal wall into the bloodstream for distribution throughout the body.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The sum of all chemical processes occurring within the body to maintain life, including building up and breaking down substances, is called
questions.explanation: Metabolism encompasses all the chemical reactions occurring within the body, including both the breakdown (catabolism) and building up (anabolism) of substances.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dietary plan for infants generally emphasises
options: highly spiced adult meals from birth
easily digestible, nutrient-dense foods appropriate to their developmental stage
large portions of tough, fibrous, hard-to-chew foods
complete avoidance of any dietary fat
questions.explanation: Infant diets prioritise easily digestible, nutrient-dense foods suited to their developing digestive systems, gradually introducing solids appropriate to age.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dietary plan for adolescents generally requires
options: increased energy, protein, and mineral intake to support rapid growth and development
complete avoidance of all dairy products
significantly reduced calorie and nutrient intake compared to younger children
identical nutrient requirements to elderly individuals
questions.explanation: Adolescents undergoing rapid growth generally require increased energy, protein, and mineral intake compared to younger children.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dietary plan for pregnant and lactating women generally requires increased intake of
options: protein, iron, calcium, and folic acid to support foetal/infant development and maternal health
no dietary changes at all compared to before pregnancy
only carbohydrates, with no other nutrient adjustments
questions.explanation: Pregnant and lactating women require increased protein, iron, calcium, and folic acid to support foetal or infant development and their own health.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dietary plan for manual workers engaged in heavy physical labour generally requires
options: higher energy (calorie) intake to match increased physical exertion
significantly reduced energy intake compared to sedentary individuals
questions.explanation: Manual workers performing heavy physical labour require higher energy intake to replace the calories expended through their strenuous work.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dietary plan for the elderly generally emphasises
options: nutrient-dense, easily digestible foods, often with reduced calorie needs due to lower activity levels
very high calorie, high-fat foods regardless of activity level
questions.explanation: Elderly individuals often need nutrient-dense, easily digestible foods, with calorie needs generally reduced due to lower activity levels and metabolism.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A therapeutic diet for a person with diabetes generally focuses on
options: maximising sugar and refined carbohydrate intake
eliminating all forms of dietary fibre
controlling carbohydrate intake and choosing foods with a lower impact on blood sugar levels
questions.explanation: Diabetic diets typically focus on managing carbohydrate intake and choosing foods that have a more moderate effect on blood glucose levels.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A therapeutic diet for a person with hypertension (high blood pressure) generally focuses on
options: eliminating all vegetables from the diet
questions.explanation: Hypertension management typically involves reducing dietary sodium (salt) intake, which can help control blood pressure levels.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A diet planned for a convalescent (someone recovering from illness) generally emphasises
options: easily digestible, nutrient-rich foods to support recovery
identical requirements to a healthy manual labourer
questions.explanation: Convalescent diets typically favour easily digestible, nutrient-rich foods that support the body's recovery process without overburdening a weakened digestive system.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A balanced diet is best described as one that
options: consists of a single food type eaten repeatedly
excludes all fats and oils entirely
provides all essential nutrients in the correct proportions needed for good health
contains only carbohydrates and no other nutrients
questions.explanation: A balanced diet supplies all essential nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water) in appropriate proportions to maintain good health.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Proteins are made up of smaller building-block units called
questions.explanation: Proteins are composed of chains of amino acids, which the body links together in specific sequences to build various proteins.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: An amino acid that the body cannot synthesise itself and must therefore obtain from the diet is called an
questions.explanation: Essential amino acids cannot be produced by the body and must be obtained through dietary protein sources.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Fats and oils are composed of fatty acids combined with a molecule of
questions.explanation: Fats and oils (triglycerides) are formed from three fatty acid chains attached to a single glycerol molecule.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Carbohydrates are broadly classified into simple sugars and more complex forms known as
questions.explanation: Complex carbohydrates, or polysaccharides such as starch, are made of many linked sugar units, unlike simple sugars (monosaccharides and disaccharides).

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The mineral most closely associated with building and maintaining strong bones and teeth is
questions.explanation: Calcium is essential for building and maintaining strong bones and teeth, alongside supporting other bodily functions like muscle contraction.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The mineral most closely associated with the formation of haemoglobin in red blood cells is
questions.explanation: Iron is a key component of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells responsible for transporting oxygen throughout the body.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The mineral essential for normal thyroid gland function, with deficiency leading to goitre, is
questions.explanation: Iodine is essential for the thyroid gland's production of hormones; deficiency can result in an enlarged thyroid gland, known as goitre.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Grain foods such as rice, maize, and wheat, which are important sources of carbohydrate, are classified as
questions.explanation: Cereals are grain crops, such as rice, maize, and wheat, providing significant amounts of dietary carbohydrate.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Plant foods such as beans, peas, and lentils, notable for their relatively high protein content among plant foods, are classified as
questions.explanation: Legumes, including beans, peas, and lentils, are valued as plant sources of protein alongside carbohydrates.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Starchy plant foods such as yam, cassava, and potato, which grow underground, are classified as
questions.explanation: Roots and tubers are underground starchy plant foods, including yam, cassava, and potato, primarily valued for their carbohydrate content.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Meat, poultry, and fish, all valued primarily for their protein content, are collectively classified as
questions.explanation: Flesh foods, including meat, poultry, and fish, are animal-derived foods valued mainly for their high-quality protein content.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Foods derived from milk, such as cheese, yoghurt, and butter, are classified as
questions.explanation: Dairy products are derived from milk and are valued especially for their protein and calcium content.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: When selecting fresh fish for purchase, a key indicator of freshness is
options: bright, clear eyes and firm flesh that springs back when pressed
dull, sunken eyes and soft, mushy flesh
questions.explanation: Fresh fish typically has bright, clear eyes and firm flesh, distinguishing it from stale fish, which shows dull eyes and soft, unresponsive flesh.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Cereals should generally be stored in conditions that are
options: cool, dry, and well-ventilated to prevent mould growth and pest infestation
exposed to direct sunlight and rain
completely airtight with high moisture content
warm and humid to encourage faster ripening
questions.explanation: Proper cereal storage in cool, dry, ventilated conditions helps prevent mould growth, insect infestation, and spoilage.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The microorganisms most commonly responsible for causing food spoilage include
options: enzymes only, with no living organisms involved
questions.explanation: Bacteria, yeasts, and moulds are the primary microorganisms responsible for the spoilage and decomposition of food.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Naturally occurring enzymes present within food can contribute to spoilage mainly by
options: continuing to break down the food's tissues and nutrients even after harvesting or slaughter
having no effect on food quality over time
preserving the food indefinitely without any other intervention
actively killing harmful microorganisms present in the food
questions.explanation: Enzymes naturally present in food continue their breakdown activity after harvesting or slaughter, contributing to spoilage if not controlled through preservation methods.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A food preservation method that removes moisture from food to inhibit microbial growth is called
questions.explanation: Dehydration removes the moisture microorganisms need to grow, extending the shelf life of the preserved food.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A food preservation method that slows microbial growth and enzyme activity by storing food at low, above-freezing temperatures is called
questions.explanation: Refrigeration slows (but does not stop) microbial growth and enzyme activity by keeping food at low, above-freezing temperatures.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A food preservation method that stops microbial growth almost entirely by storing food at temperatures well below freezing is called
questions.explanation: Freezing preserves food by lowering its temperature well below the freezing point, effectively halting most microbial growth and slowing enzyme activity.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A food preservation method that seals food in airtight containers and applies heat to destroy microorganisms is called
questions.explanation: Canning combines heat treatment with airtight sealing, destroying microorganisms and preventing recontamination for extended shelf life.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A heat treatment process that destroys most harmful microorganisms in a liquid, such as milk, without fully sterilising it, is called
questions.explanation: Pasteurization uses controlled heating to destroy most harmful microorganisms while preserving more of the food's quality than full sterilisation.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A heat treatment process that destroys virtually all microorganisms, including their spores, is called
questions.explanation: Sterilization uses higher heat and longer exposure than pasteurization to destroy nearly all microorganisms, including resistant spores.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A food preservation method using substances such as salt, sugar, or specific chemical additives to inhibit microbial growth is called
questions.explanation: Chemical preservation uses substances like salt, sugar, vinegar, or approved additives to create conditions unfavourable for microbial growth.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A traditional food preservation method that exposes food to smoke, both drying it and depositing preservative compounds, is called
questions.explanation: Smoking preserves food through a combination of drying and depositing antimicrobial compounds from the smoke onto the food's surface.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The protein found in wheat flour that gives dough its elastic, stretchy structure, essential for bread making, is called
questions.explanation: Gluten, formed when wheat flour is mixed with water, provides the elastic structure that traps gas bubbles and gives bread its characteristic texture.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A raising method that incorporates air into a mixture through vigorous physical action, such as whisking egg whites, is classified as
questions.explanation: Mechanical raising methods, such as whisking or creaming, incorporate air physically into a mixture, which expands during cooking to provide lift.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A raising method that uses substances such as baking powder or bicarbonate of soda, which release gas through a chemical reaction, is classified as
questions.explanation: Chemical raising agents, like baking powder and bicarbonate of soda, release carbon dioxide gas through chemical reactions, causing mixtures to rise.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A raising method that relies on living yeast fermenting sugars and producing carbon dioxide gas is classified as
questions.explanation: Biological raising uses living yeast, which ferments sugars in the dough and produces carbon dioxide gas, causing the dough to rise.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Fresh fruits and vegetables should generally be stored in conditions that
options: involve tightly sealed, airless containers for all types
maintain appropriate cool temperatures and humidity to slow ripening and decay
expose them to continuous direct sunlight
maximise warmth and dryness to speed up ripening
questions.explanation: Most fresh fruits and vegetables keep best in cool, appropriately humid conditions that slow the natural processes of ripening and decay.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Fats and oils used in cooking should generally be stored away from
options: cool, dark conditions, which help preserve them
light, heat, and air, which can cause them to become rancid
airtight containers, which best preserve freshness
questions.explanation: Exposure to light, heat, and air accelerates the oxidation of fats and oils, causing them to become rancid; proper storage minimises this exposure.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A common structural feature of cereal grains is their outer protective layer, known as the
options: husk removed entirely before any processing
questions.explanation: The bran is the tough outer protective layer of a cereal grain, rich in fibre, surrounding the starchy endosperm and nutrient-rich germ.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The nutrient-rich inner part of a cereal grain, often removed during refined milling, is called the
questions.explanation: The germ is the nutrient-dense embryo of the grain, often removed along with the bran during the refining process, reducing the nutritional value of refined grains.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A major reason meat, poultry, and fish require careful, prompt refrigeration after purchase is that they are
options: unaffected by temperature under any circumstances
the only foods that never require refrigeration
naturally resistant to all microbial spoilage
highly perishable and susceptible to rapid microbial spoilage
questions.explanation: Flesh foods are highly perishable, providing an ideal environment for microbial growth, making prompt and proper refrigeration essential to prevent spoilage.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: The main purpose of blanching vegetables briefly in boiling water before freezing them is to
options: fully cook the vegetables before freezing
add extra moisture content to the vegetables
destroy enzymes that would otherwise continue to degrade quality during frozen storage
questions.explanation: Blanching briefly destroys enzymes that would otherwise continue breaking down the vegetable's quality, colour, and texture during frozen storage.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A key sign that canned food may be unsafe to eat, indicating possible bacterial contamination, is
options: a bulging or swollen can lid
a can that is cool to the touch
a can with a clear, undamaged label
a can stored in a cool, dry cupboard
questions.explanation: A bulging or swollen can lid can indicate gas production from bacterial contamination inside, signalling that the contents may be unsafe to consume.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Wheat flour used for bread-making generally requires a
options: higher gluten (protein) content, to provide the necessary elastic structure
lower gluten content than flour used for delicate cakes
questions.explanation: Bread-making flour ('strong' flour) has a higher gluten content, providing the elastic structure needed to trap gas and support a well-risen loaf.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Cake flour generally has a
options: higher gluten content than bread flour
identical gluten content to bread flour
lower gluten (protein) content than bread flour, producing a softer, more tender texture
questions.explanation: Cake ('soft') flour has a lower gluten content than bread flour, helping to produce the lighter, more tender texture desired in cakes.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: An efficient kitchen layout generally organises work into distinct zones for
options: storage, preparation, and cooking, to allow a smooth workflow
decoration purposes only, with no practical function
a single combined zone with no logical separation
cooking only, with storage and preparation done elsewhere entirely
questions.explanation: A well-planned kitchen separates storage, preparation, and cooking zones, supporting an efficient, logical workflow from raw ingredients to finished dishes.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A key kitchen safety practice to prevent burns and scalds is to
options: handle hot pans with wet cloths
ignore the use of any protective equipment
turn pot handles inward and use dry oven gloves when handling hot items
leave pot handles extending outward over the edge of the cooker
questions.explanation: Turning pot handles inward reduces the risk of accidental knocks, while dry oven gloves protect hands from burns when handling hot cookware.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A key kitchen safety practice to prevent slips and falls is to
options: clean up spills immediately and keep floors dry
encourage running within the kitchen area
keep the kitchen floor cluttered with equipment
leave spilled liquids on the floor until the end of the day
questions.explanation: Promptly cleaning spills and keeping floors dry significantly reduces the risk of slips and falls in a busy kitchen environment.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Good kitchen hygiene practices generally include
options: storing raw meat above ready-to-eat foods in the refrigerator
ignoring expiry dates on perishable items
handling raw and cooked foods with the same unwashed utensils
regular handwashing and keeping food preparation surfaces clean
questions.explanation: Regular handwashing and clean preparation surfaces are fundamental hygiene practices that help prevent cross-contamination and foodborne illness.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cooking method that involves cooking food fully submerged in liquid at a rolling temperature of 100°C is called
questions.explanation: Boiling cooks food fully immersed in liquid heated to its boiling point (100°C at sea level).

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cooking method that involves slow cooking food in a small amount of liquid over a long period, tenderising tougher cuts, is called
questions.explanation: Stewing slowly cooks food in a smaller amount of liquid over an extended time, effectively tenderising tougher ingredients.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cooking method that involves gently cooking food in liquid kept just below boiling point, often used for delicate items like eggs or fish, is called
questions.explanation: Poaching uses gently simmering liquid kept below boiling point, suitable for delicate foods that would break apart under a rolling boil.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cooking method that involves cooking food using the vapour produced by boiling water, without direct contact with the liquid, is called
questions.explanation: Steaming cooks food using hot water vapour, keeping it out of direct contact with the boiling liquid itself.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dry cooking method that cooks food using hot, dry air within an enclosed oven is called
questions.explanation: Baking uses hot, dry air circulating within an enclosed oven to cook food, commonly used for bread, cakes, and pastries.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dry cooking method traditionally used to cook larger cuts of meat using hot, dry air, often with added fat for basting, is called
questions.explanation: Roasting cooks larger food items, especially meat, using dry heat, often basted with fat to keep the surface from drying out excessively.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A dry cooking method that cooks food quickly using direct, intense heat from above or below, such as a grill element, is called
questions.explanation: Grilling exposes food to intense, direct radiant heat, cooking it quickly while often producing a characteristic charred or browned surface.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cooking method that fully immerses food in hot oil or fat, often producing a crisp exterior, is called
questions.explanation: Deep frying fully submerges food in hot oil, cooking it quickly while producing a crisp, browned exterior.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cooking method that cooks food in a small, shallow amount of oil or fat in a pan is called
questions.explanation: Shallow frying uses only a small amount of oil in a pan, cooking food primarily on one surface at a time before turning.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cooking method that quickly cooks small pieces of food over high heat while constantly moving them in a small amount of oil, typically in a wok, is called
questions.explanation: Stir frying rapidly cooks small, evenly cut pieces of food over high heat, using constant movement and minimal oil, typically in a wok.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A key advantage of moist cooking methods such as stewing is that they
options: require no liquid of any kind
always cook food faster than dry methods
prevent any loss of water-soluble nutrients
can effectively tenderise tougher cuts of meat over a longer cooking time
questions.explanation: Moist methods like stewing use prolonged gentle cooking in liquid to break down connective tissue, effectively tenderising tougher cuts of meat.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A key disadvantage of boiling vegetables for an extended time is that it can
options: increase the vitamin content of the vegetables
cause significant loss of water-soluble vitamins into the cooking liquid
have no effect on the nutrient content at all
make the vegetables firmer and crunchier
questions.explanation: Prolonged boiling can leach water-soluble vitamins, such as vitamin C and some B vitamins, out of vegetables and into the surrounding cooking liquid.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A pastry made by rubbing fat into flour to form a short, crumbly texture, commonly used for pie cases and tarts, is called
questions.explanation: Shortcrust pastry is made by rubbing fat into flour, producing a short, crumbly texture ideal for pie and tart bases.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A pastry made by folding layers of fat and dough together repeatedly, producing a light, flaky, layered texture, is called
questions.explanation: Flaky pastry is created through repeated folding of fat within the dough, producing distinct light, flaky layers when baked.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A pastry made by cooking flour and fat together in liquid before beating in eggs, producing a light, hollow structure used for items like éclairs, is called
questions.explanation: Choux pastry involves cooking a flour-fat-liquid mixture before beating in eggs, producing a light, airy dough that puffs into hollow shapes like éclairs and profiteroles.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cake-making method in which fat is worked into flour before other ingredients are added, commonly used for plain cakes, is called the
questions.explanation: The rubbed-in method combines fat and flour by rubbing them together, similar to shortcrust pastry, commonly used for simpler, plainer cakes.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cake-making method in which fat and sugar are beaten together until light and fluffy before other ingredients are added, commonly used for richer cakes, is called the
questions.explanation: The creamed method beats fat and sugar together to incorporate air, producing a light texture suited to richer cake recipes.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cake-making method that relies mainly on whisking eggs and sugar together to incorporate air, often producing a light sponge with little or no fat, is called the
questions.explanation: The whisked method incorporates air primarily through vigorously beating eggs and sugar, producing a light sponge texture, often with minimal or no added fat.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A cake-making method in which fat, sugar, and liquid ingredients are melted together before being combined with dry ingredients, commonly used for gingerbread, is called the
questions.explanation: The melted method combines melted fat, sugar, and liquid with dry ingredients, commonly used for dense cakes like gingerbread.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A sauce made from a base of butter and flour (roux) cooked with milk, without browning the roux, is called a
questions.explanation: A white sauce (béchamel) is made from a roux of butter and flour cooked briefly without browning, then combined with milk.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A sauce made from a roux that has been cooked until browned, typically combined with stock, is called a
questions.explanation: A brown sauce uses a roux cooked to a darker colour before liquid (often stock) is added, giving it a deeper flavour and colour than a white sauce.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A sauce formed by combining two normally unmixable liquids, such as oil and vinegar, into a stable mixture, is called an
questions.explanation: Emulsified sauces, such as mayonnaise, combine typically unmixable liquids (like oil and vinegar) into a stable blended mixture, often using an emulsifying agent like egg yolk.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A thick liquid dish, typically made by simmering meat, vegetables, or other ingredients in stock, is generally called a
questions.explanation: Soups are liquid-based dishes made by simmering various ingredients, such as meat, vegetables, or grains, in a flavourful stock or broth.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A soup that has been passed through a sieve or blended to produce a smooth, thickened consistency is called a
questions.explanation: Puréed (cream) soups are blended or sieved to achieve a smooth, thick texture, unlike clear soups which retain a thin, transparent consistency.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A clear, well-flavoured soup made by carefully clarifying a rich stock is called a
questions.explanation: Consommé is a clear soup produced by carefully clarifying a rich stock, typically using egg whites to remove impurities, resulting in a crystal-clear liquid.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Traditional local dishes taught in a Foods and Nutrition curriculum are important mainly because they
options: reflect cultural food heritage while applying learned nutritional and culinary principles
require no cooking skill to prepare
are always less nutritious than foreign dishes
have no connection to nutritional science at all
questions.explanation: Studying traditional local dishes connects cultural heritage with practical application of nutrition science and culinary techniques learned in the course.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: When planning a kitchen work triangle (the relationship between the sink, cooker, and refrigerator), the main goal is to
options: eliminate the need for a refrigerator in the kitchen
maximise the distance between all three areas
place all three appliances in exactly the same spot
minimise unnecessary movement between these key work areas
questions.explanation: An efficient kitchen work triangle arrangement minimises the distance and movement needed between the sink, cooker, and refrigerator, improving workflow efficiency.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Adequate ventilation in a kitchen is important mainly to
options: eliminate the need for proper food storage
remove excess heat, steam, and cooking odours
prevent any air circulation at all
questions.explanation: Good kitchen ventilation removes excess heat, steam, and odours generated during cooking, improving comfort and air quality.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A key precaution when using a gas cooker in the kitchen is to
options: store flammable materials directly beside the cooker
block all ventilation to conserve heat
ignore any smell of gas, assuming it is harmless
ensure proper ventilation and check for gas leaks regularly
questions.explanation: Gas cookers require good ventilation and regular leak checks as essential safety precautions to prevent the buildup of hazardous gas.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: A basic knife safety practice in the kitchen is to
options: always cut toward the body for better visibility
store knives loosely in a drawer with other utensils
use only extremely blunt knives for all cutting tasks
always cut away from the body and keep knives sharp for safer, more controlled cuts
questions.explanation: Cutting away from the body and using well-sharpened knives (which require less force and are less likely to slip) are basic, essential knife safety practices.

questions.subject: Foods and Nutrition
questions.text: Cross-contamination in the kitchen is best prevented by
options: using the same chopping board for all food types without washing it
washing hands only at the start of meal preparation
using separate chopping boards and utensils for raw meat and ready-to-eat foods
storing raw meat directly next to cooked food in the refrigerator
questions.explanation: Using separate chopping boards and utensils for raw meat and ready-to-eat foods, along with regular handwashing, are key measures to prevent cross-contamination.
